description: Turn one sunscreen photo into a social media video for TikTok, a square feed post, and a wide screen. Pick the shape, then download it and post.
h1: Social Media Video Sizes for TikTok and Instagram
lead: Turn one sunscreen photo into a tall phone ad, a square feed post, and a wide screen. Social media video sizes are what you pick so the tube fills the placement. Make each shape as its own file, with the tube kept large.
secondary_keywords: square ads for the Facebook feed
summary: A small shop can cover a phone, a feed, and a wide screen without guessing the shape. Make the tall 9:16 file first for phone ads, add a square for the feed, and make 16:9 only when the screen is wide.

sections.h2: Eight Ad Styles That Make a Shopper Stop
paras: Pick the style that gives a shopper one reason to stop on the sunscreen tube. The shape comes after that reason is clear. A tall phone and a square feed can share the same idea.
Time the Cap Click. A cap click can be the whole clip. Time that click to a track shoppers already know, and end when the cap is shut. Pick a track they still hear this week.
Pack the Tube in a Beach Bag. Show how the tube fits in a beach bag, and let the spoken line name that one motion. A long lecture can wait. The shopper asked how it packs, so show that.
Pull the Tube Out at the Beach. A day-with-the-bag clip sells the moment the tube comes out at the beach. Start on the open bag, and let that moment be the whole story.
Answer One Makeup Comment. A reply to one comment, such as whether it sits under makeup, gives the detail they asked for. Keep the tube in frame, and keep the answer large enough to read.
Compare Two Sunscreen Tubes. A shopper comparing two sunscreen tubes will pause for the cap, the feel, and the size. Say those three, and leave the tube in the frame the whole time.
Show the Fill and the Spray. Show the fill, the seal, and the first spray. That sequence gives people a step they can follow, with the tube kept large.
Set the Tube in Soft Light. Soft light on a real surface can carry the mood on your profile, often as a square. The label still has to match the product page.
Land One Joke, Then the Tube. One joke, then the sunscreen tube, easy to see. Keep the item in view once the joke has landed.
Each placement gets a file that already fills its screen. Make that shape on its own, so the sunscreen tube stays large.
A wide YouTube screen gets a 16:9 file, and Shorts get a tall one that fills the phone. The tall file is its own job. See [YouTube Shorts](page:plat-youtube-shorts).
Instagram wants a square tube photo in the scrolling feed, and Stories want the tall file. A square dropped into that tall slot leaves bars. Make the feed file and the tall file as two jobs.
A 9:16 file fills the TikTok screen, so the tube stays large. A wide clip on an upright phone shrinks to a strip. Build the tall file with [AI UGC video ads](page:video-ads).
LinkedIn can take a square or a wide post, which gives people room to pause and read. Keep the words large, and keep the claim identical to the product page.
Facebook can use a square in the feed and a tall file for the full-screen spot. Build that Facebook file on its own so the sunscreen tube stays large.

paras: The sunscreen tube stays in the part of the screen shoppers can actually see. Match the shape to the screen, then check what the app covers. Confirm the crop in the ad manager. These are shapes, not a promise of one pixel size. Shoppers often ask for a 1080x1920 phone file or a 1080x1080 square, and those are common exports of the tall and square shapes.
16:9 fills a laptop, a longer demo, or a desktop feed. A full phone screen wants the tall file instead.
9:16 is the tall shape, and it is the one that fills a phone. Names sit at the top. Like and share sit on the right. Keep the sunscreen tube and any words in the middle, clear of those buttons.
1:1 fills a Facebook or Instagram feed, a swipeable row of cards, and the spots where the placement is still open. A still photo can use this shape too.

4:3 is a little wider than a square, and 3:4 is a little taller. Use them when a placement lists that shape. For other jobs, pick 9:16, 1:1, or 16:9 on the setup screen. For current Shorts file rules, see [YouTube Shorts size rules](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/16041697?hl=en-GB).

paras: One sunscreen photo can feed a tall file and a square file. They are two jobs, and each one shows its credit cost before it starts.
Open on the cap when other sunscreen ads open on the label. That gives your file a different first second. Use a track that still shows up where your buyers scroll.
You set the gap between the first word and the product, and that pace is yours. For this tube, the gap might be one second. Put that gap in your own script.
You can post without standing on camera. Pick an AI actor from the [actor library](page:ai-actors), or show only the tube. Anyone on screen is an AI actor you chose for the shop.
The size on the product page can become the spoken line in a tall file, next to the photo you already took. That page is enough to begin. See [URL to video](page:url-to-video).

sections.h2: How Four Shops Split the Shapes
paras: A home shop gets a 9:16 file and a 1:1 file from the sunscreen page. They skip an evening of cutting one video apart. They run the file that fills the placement.
A skincare shop gets a second opening for the same tube without a new photo. They keep the photo and the offer, change the first line, and run both files for the same people.
A solo seller leaves the frame on the tube and adds a spoken line. They post the tall file where the phone screen is full.
A shop that sells in two languages keeps the same tube and replaces the spoken line. The shape stays the one that fills that placement.

sections.h2: Which Style Fits What You Sell
paras: Match the pace to the product, and keep the label easy to see. Keep any joke clear of the label too.
Land the Joke, Then the Label. Short jokes still have to sell the item. Land the laugh, then leave the sunscreen label readable, with the tube in frame for the rest of the clip.
Show the Sunscreen in a Routine. A routine or a texture shot shows the sunscreen in context. Hold the real tube next to the screen and check the shade before you post.
Snap One Case Shut. One motion is enough, such as a case snapping shut. Keep the words in the middle, where the buttons leave them readable on a phone.
Show the Piece Hung, Then Worn. Shoppers see the piece hung up and then worn, in the same color in both frames. Show the back only when the photo you took includes the back.
Answer One Packing Question. A teaching clip answers one real question, such as how the item packs. The product stays easy to see while the answer plays.
Leave the Frame on the Product. Faceless updates run without you on camera. Leave the frame on the product, add captions, and let a voice read the offer. Match that offer to the product page.

sections.h2: What the Editor Handles for You
paras: The chores that used to mean three apps now sit in one pass. You still choose the line and the shape.
You get an opening that fits the tube, such as the cap in the first second, and a track that matches a slow shot. You still pick the line. Pick one that fits this season.
A brand that never shows a face can still have a spoken line. Leave the frame on the product, and put that line on the caption track.
Cuts can land on a beat you pick from the music library. A cap click can sit on that same beat.
You get a script you can edit. It is written from the product page, like a reply to a shopper. Change the line before the job starts.

A photo you already took of the sunscreen tube is enough to start the clip. [AI image to video](page:image-to-video) is the way in. A product link is the other door. It helps when the page already lists the size and the texture.
Finish in one place. Captions, the spoken voice, and the song live in the editor. You can change how the words look, and you can make several openings from the same photo.
You spend your time on the shape and the line. The frame-by-frame trim is already handled for you.
A photo of the whole sunscreen tube is the usual start. A product link works when the page already shows that tube. Bring your own clip when you want the pace of something you filmed.
Mark the second where the label has to be readable. The rest of the timing can flex around that one second.
Pick one shape for this job: 9:16, 1:1, 16:9, 4:3, or 3:4. A second shape is a separate job.
The spoken line sits in the middle, clear of the bottom and the right edge, where the app covers words. A song can wait until this pass looks right.
Download the file. Nothing is stamped on it. Play it on your phone before you pay to run it, and check that the tube is still in the middle.
A video is 24 credits for 6 seconds, 40 for 10, 60 for 15, or 120 for 30. Starter is $24.50 a month for 200 credits. Pro is $35 for 300 credits, and Premium is $63 for 600.

paras: Three shapes cover the screens a small shop actually buys. Use 9:16 for a full phone screen, 1:1 for the scrolling feed, and 16:9 for wide screens. Use 4:3 or 3:4 only when that placement lists them. Keep the sunscreen tube in the middle.
A script, captions, a spoken voice, and a song can be included. Another shape is another job. If a job fails, the credits come back.

faq.q: Can I resize a landscape video to vertical?
faq.a: Yes. Make the tall version as its own job, with the words placed for a phone. Watch that tall file before you retire the wide one.

faq.q: Can I post without showing my face?
faq.a: Yes. Keep the frame on the product and use a spoken line, or put an AI actor in the shot when the ad needs a person.

faq.q: Are the music and the spoken voice safe to use in an ad?
faq.a: Yes for the tracks in the music library and for the voice this product generates. A track you brought from somewhere else is yours to clear. Before you pay to run the ad, confirm that the placement allows that library track.

faq.q: Can the edit follow the music?
faq.a: Yes. A cap click can sit on a beat you chose. If the cuts get so fast that the label blurs, slow the clip down. The tube has to stay readable.

faq.q: Can I start from a product page or a short article?
faq.a: Yes. A page that already lists the size and the texture can supply the spoken line. You can change that line before the job starts. A photo you took of the tube is enough when the page is thin.

faq.q: Can I change how the words on screen look?
faq.a: Yes. The words can use your shop color, and they can sit still instead of moving. Set that before you spend the credits.

faq.q: Can the same ad run in another language?
faq.a: Yes. A shop that sells the same tube in Spanish needs a second file. The scene can stay. The spoken line is the part you replace.

faq.q: Which shape should a small shop make first?
faq.a: Start with 9:16 when the first placement is a full phone screen. Add a square when the same offer also sits in a scrolling feed. Make the wide 16:9 file only when the screen itself is wide.

cta_title: Make the Right Size, Then Post It
cta_lead: You get a file that fills the screen you are buying. Start from a sunscreen photo or a product link, and pick 9:16, 1:1, or 16:9.
